title: Shoftim: judges at the gates (Deuteronomy 16:18)
hookLine: judges in every town; Hasidic teachers read the gates as eyes, ears and mouth

lines: TO SETTLE IT, GO TO THE GATE.
cards: Where would you go to settle a family dispute in the world of the Bible? Not a building with columns. The gate.
In the Bible, a town gate is more than a door in the wall. Elders sit there. Deals are witnessed there.
In the book of Ruth, Boaz goes up to the gate, sits down, and settles a family matter in front of ten elders.
Everything that comes into the town, people, goods, news, trouble, comes through the gate, and whoever sits there decides what to do about it. That's where the new portion begins.

teach.b: The first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates." Shoftim means judges, and it names the portion. The plain sense is civic.
Every town needs courts, and people to enforce what courts decide, right where life passes through. Justice shouldn't be a long trip to a distant capital.
It should sit at your own gate. But notice the odd little word thee.
In Hebrew, lecha: for yourself. Judges for yourself? Hasidic masters, building on earlier mystics, read the verse inward.
A person is a town too, they said, with gates of their own: the eyes, the ears, the mouth, and some add the nostrils.
Everything that enters you comes through those gates, what you look at, what you listen to, what you take in. And what leaves you goes out through one of them: what you say.
So set judges at your gates. Not to shut them; a town with its gates welded shut starves. But to notice what's coming in and going out, and to decide.
And the calendar helps. Shoftim is usually read around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, a season set aside for taking stock.
A portion about courts at the gates arrives just as people start judging their own year.

how: Shoftim is usually read in synagogues around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, and Hasidic and other teachers often use its opening verse to speak about guarding the eyes, ears and mouth as part of the season's self-examination.

games.q: the verse says judges and officers shalt thou make thee. Hasidic teachers ask: why for yourself? what do they answer?
o: a person has gates too: eyes, ears and mouth.
games.why: they read a person as a town, with gates for what comes in and goes out, each needing a judge.

practice: Notice your eyes resting, your ears taking in whatever sound is here, your mouth closed.

Then look back over the last day: what came in through your eyes or ears that you'd rather not have let in, and what went out of your mouth that you'd take back? Pick one gate, just one, and let its judge sit there quietly.

wordCard.voice: Shoftim. Judges. The name of the portion, from its first command: judges and officers in all your gates.
